results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

All 107 outliner summaries match the controlling idea of the spec paragraph they align to, in spec order (callouts matched to the roadmap and thesis statement). Tool 2 ¶5 and Tool 10 ¶5 carry extra template fields beside their explanation, still within the card's unit.
The two phrases (undecided question; what the sixteen cards are) are the two halves of p001's single controlling idea.
p047's controlling idea itself joins when to fill the card with the key-derivation and timeout rules; one idea as declared.
The opening sentence on keeping both providers is a one-sentence bridge from the example (p090 names that decision); the paragraph's idea is staleness and the half-yearly re-read.

Every unit serves a reader using the page: the finder table and its note trace to S1, the connection section to S3, and each card's six units to S2; introduction and conclusion carry the thesis and the upkeep habits.

The lookup table is introduced by its heading and ordering sentence; Figure 1 has a caption and the following plain-words paragraph; each blank template is labelled and each filled example is followed by an explanation unit, except the two noted below.

results.quote: None of the three figures is a bank account of the studio's, and Larkfield holds none of them.
results.finding: The sentence that explains the filled table speaks of 'three figures' after a four-row table (the fourth is the refund), so the reader cannot tell which rows it means. Both flow readers stopped here. Name the three amounts (€117.47, €1.92, €0.61) or say 'the three amounts of the sale'.

results.quote: At 5 requests a second, about 200,000 renewals need 11.1 hours
results.finding: The explanation uses 200,000 renewals right after a table that gives the peak as about 357,000, without saying that 200,000 is the Adyen share; both flow readers could not reconcile the figures. Say 'the about 200,000 renewals on Adyen'.

Introduction boundaries open as declared (elaboration 'The filled examples use Larkfield', sequence 'Three conventions hold', emphasis 'Start with three'); section boundaries are carried by the numbered headings and the finder table, which is what a reference page needs; within each card the bold labels (What it records / The template / When and who / Larkfield example / Taught in) express the declared elaboration, sequence and example relationships; the conclusion opens with a summary and hands off to [[glossary]].

Both flow readers describe the declared grouping: orientation, the finder table, the connection map, then the sixteen cards in the order of the book's parts, then upkeep; neither marks any section's position unclear.

results.quote: **Keel** is Larkfield's 2027 program of eight decisions, K1 to K8; a card names the decision it carries out.
results.finding: The examples then cite K2, K3, K4, K6, K7 as bare codes (e.g. 'goes to the sweep of decision K2' as the owner path in Tool 7) and neither reader could tell what they decided. Give each code a few words where it is first used, or a one-line key here (mind the 8,050-word limit; the duplicated fiction disclaimer in Sources and Evidence can pay for it).
results.corroborated_by: flow reader A item 3 (Keel decisions as bare codes); flow reader B item 3 (Keel decisions used by number without a key)

results.quote: The record that counts as the truth is the one that wins when two records disagree.
results.finding: The page's central field is defined narrowly, but Tools 3, 13 and 16 fill it with a rehearsal, the signals watched in a paced run and a measure of whether a decision worked. Both readers stopped to reconcile the two; a reader filling a card cannot tell what belongs in the field. Widen the definition (the record a doubt is settled against: a provider record, a report line, or for a plan or decision the rehearsal or measure that shows it worked).
results.corroborated_by: flow reader A item 3 ('Record that is the truth' stretches beyond its definition); flow reader B item 3 ('Record that is the truth' is stretched in places)

results.draft_locus: Find the Card for the Question on Your Desk ¶1
results.quote: | How would we leave this provider? | [Tool 15](#tool-15): Provider exit plan card | X | [[tokenization-vaulting-and-pci]] |
results.finding: Right after 'The cards are numbered in the order of the book's parts', the table files Tool 15 under Part X with a Part V chapter, and Tool 16 under 'all' with one chapter; both readers doubted the stated order. The card never says why it sits in Part X (the spec's reason: the Part X chapter tells the reader to keep it beside the comparison card). Say so in the table or in Tool 15's 'What it records'.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader A item 3 (Tool 15 breaks the stated order); flow reader B item 3 (Finder table: Tool 15 sits in Part X but teaches from tokenization-vaulting-and-pci)

results.finding: The filled example does not use the template's fields (record that is the truth, scheduler, per failure, message trigger, deadline, owner): it expands one row into a Situation/Action/Limit table and moves the rest into the following prose, so a reader learning to fill the card must map it by hand. Both readers named Tool 10 (they also named Tools 2 and 11, whose examples map more directly and are not failed). Keep the schedule table but label it as the 'Per failure' and 'Deadline' rows, or add the remaining fields as rows.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader A item 3 (Templates and examples don't always match, 'Situation / Action / Limit' in Tool 10); flow reader B item 3 (Tool 10 'Situation | Action | Limit')

results.quote: The cards use terms such as idempotency key, clearing account, payout return and PCI scope with little or no definition.
results.finding: The admission that terms go undefined, and the pointer to the glossary, come only after the reader has met every term; both readers needed it at the start. The p106 hand-off can stay where it is; a one-clause glossary pointer in the introduction (e.g. in the conventions) fixes the reader's problem without reordering units. The spec changelog already lists moving it as an open note for the author.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader A item 3 (The glossary pointer comes too late); flow reader B item 3 (The glossary pointer comes at the very end)

results.finding: The template says every attempt for the event sends the same key, yet the example key ends in an attempt number; the following paragraph resolves it only on a re-read. Say in the example that the business event is one scheduled attempt, so resends of that attempt share its key. Reported by one reader only.

Points both readers raised but judged not to hinder use of the page: the KEY POINTS callout and ¶1 repeat the thesis (house format places the thesis in both); people outside the cast list (Bram de Wit, Ravi Shah, Daniel Osei) are introduced in context; Tool 7 'When and who' restates the template (AC-2's reader relied on it); Tools 7 and 9 'When and who' name no card owner, but both templates carry an owner row; the starter cards are scattered by part order but named by tool number in the introduction; the £0.03 rounding line and the repeated fiction disclaimer in Sources are minor.

results.quote: Replay the Payout That Bounced against the card.
results.finding: The named incidents (the Payout That Bounced, the Unexplained €0.4 Million, the Double Charge, the Silent Webhook, the Frozen Studios) are used as known names with no introduction or link on this page; a reader arriving from the finder table at one card has not met them. Link each to its chapter, or to the failure-patterns page, at first use.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader A item 3 (Incidents are named as if I already knew them); flow reader B item 3 (Named incidents appear as if known)

results.finding: Card-level terms (idempotency key, PCI scope) are defined at their card; Larkfield, its people and Keel are introduced before the cards; remaining payments terms are the book's own, taught in the linked chapters.
Opens with a direct, disputable statement and says what the page gives and how each card is laid out; none of the weak patterns.
Does not open with 'in conclusion', end on a rephrased thesis or hold body evidence; the three habits are the spec's declared closing and need all sixteen cards.
'The sixteen cards ask one question sixteen times' states what no single card states, and 'A stale card is the undecided question again' says why upkeep matters, followed by the three habits.
'A stale card is the undecided question again' returns to the opening claim that a team which cannot write down the record, the owner and the date has not decided the question.

The intro reader predicted sixteen cards grouped by the book's parts, each with the decision, a blank template, when and who, a filled Larkfield example and its chapter, running from the payment state card to the exit plan and decision record; fictional Larkfield material to be replaced; and understood the truth-record/owner/date shape and the three starter cards (Tools 2, 7, 6). Their doubts (full sequence, card vs tool) do not remove the substance.

The reader picked the idempotency key card (idempotency-and-retries) for the re-run job and the payout exception card (payouts-and-money-movement) for the returned payouts, with the reasons expected, and named the three things every card asks for. Their note that the page also recommends three starter cards is a caveat, not a gap.

The reader built the key from order 8841 and the refund request's own identity so every attempt and click sends the same key, ruled out a per-call/attempt/click random value, and after a timeout read the provider's record or resent the same key, never a new one. Matches expected.
